questions.prompt: With no types listed, when does a pull_request workflow run?
choices: When the pull request is opened, reopened, or its head branch is updated
questions.explain: The defaults are opened, synchronize, and reopened. Anything else, such as labelled, needs an explicit types list.

questions.prompt: You add types: [labeled]. What happens to the default behaviour?
choices: Labelling is added to the defaults
Naming types replaces the defaults, so only labelled runs it
It runs on every activity type
questions.explain: types replaces the default set, so list every type you want the workflow to run for.

questions.prompt: What does a pull_request run check out for an open, mergeable pull request?
choices: The merge of the head into the base
questions.explain: You test the merged result, which is what would land. That is why base branch changes can break your run.

questions.prompt: Which pattern matches page.js and page.jsx, but not page.jsxx?
questions.explain: ? means zero or one of the preceding character, so the x is optional.

choices: Everything under releases/, including alpha branches
Everything under releases/ except those ending in -alpha
questions.explain: Order decides: the negation comes after the positive match, so it wins. Reversed, nothing would be excluded.

questions.prompt: A workflow filters only on paths. Someone pushes a tag. Does it run?
choices: Yes, if a changed file matches
No, path filters are not evaluated for tag pushes
Only if the tag matches a branch name
questions.explain: Path filters do not apply to tag pushes, which is a common surprise in release workflows.

questions.prompt: You define both branches and paths for one event. When does the workflow run?
choices: When the branch matches, paths are advisory
questions.explain: Branch and path filters combine with AND: both must be satisfied.

questions.prompt: Why might the Run workflow button be missing for a workflow_dispatch workflow?
choices: The workflow file is not on the default branch
It has never been run by the API
questions.explain: The file must exist on the default branch for the button to appear.

questions.prompt: A schedule is written without timezone. In what zone does it run?
choices: The zone of the last committer
questions.explain: Schedules are UTC unless a timezone is given as an IANA name such as America/New_York.

questions.prompt: A daily 02:30 schedule with a timezone meets a spring-forward change, when 02:30 does not exist. What happens?
choices: The run is skipped that day
It advances to the next valid time, 03:00
It runs twice the next day
questions.explain: Skipped local times advance to the next valid time, so the run happens at 03:00.

questions.prompt: What is the shortest interval a scheduled workflow can use?
questions.explain: Five minutes is the documented minimum, and busy periods can delay a run anyway.

questions.prompt: What context does pull_request_target run in?
choices: The merge commit of the pull request
The base repository's default branch, with secrets and a writable token
A sandbox with no repository access
questions.explain: It runs privileged, using the workflow file from your default branch rather than the contributor's merge commit.

questions.prompt: Which task is pull_request_target actually meant for?
choices: Labelling or commenting on a pull request from a fork
questions.explain: It exists so a workflow can react to a fork's pull request, which the read-only pull_request run cannot do.

questions.prompt: Why is checking out the pull request head inside pull_request_target dangerous?
choices: A stranger's code then runs with your secrets and write access
The merge commit does not exist
questions.explain: That combination is the pwn request: untrusted code executing in a privileged context, risking secrets and cache poisoning.

questions.prompt: You must build contributor code and post a result that needs write access. What is the safe shape?
choices: One pull_request_target workflow that does both
Two workflows: an untrusted build on pull_request, then a trusted one that reads its output
questions.explain: Splitting keeps untrusted code away from the privileged step, which is the pattern the security module builds.
